newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian economy seen limp despite inflation drop.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian economy seen limp despite inflation drop.

text.p: Nigeria's military government is reporting success in reducing inflation and restoring economic stability, but the kind of growth that will make a difference in the lives of its people appears elusive.

About halfway through the year, experts say the economy remains stagnant and initial forecasts for of rapid growth that followed the 1997 fiscal budget announcement in January is turning out to be a mirage.

The leading business newspaper's mid-year review of the economy published on Tuesday said experts saw a major slowdown in economic activity, mainly due to the military government's squeeze on public spending.
"The general thrust of the experts' submission was that six months into the year, the economy is not showing any noticeable signs of growth," it said.
"Nigerians, they argue, are also not well off as average real income per head and gross domestic product -- value of goods and services produced are still below expectation," it said.

The survey saw employment moving from bad to worse, consumer purchasing power down and the oil industry in trouble from lack of government funding while a persistent shortage of fuel supplies threatened industrial crisis.
Africa's most populous nation has been in crisis since the army annulled the 1993 presidential vote.
Sanctions by Western trading partners because of lack of democracy and alleged human rights abuses have severely curtailed foreign investments.

General Sani Abacha, an infantry officer who seized power in the chaos that greeted the annulment, managed to halt the economic freefall by the end of 1996 when inflation fell to about 25 percent from nearly 80 percent a year earlier.
Finance minister Anthony Ani said last week April inflation was down to 18.5 percent, but official sources say the actual level is closer to 21.4 percent.
Abacha's 1997 budget was also disappointing when he failed to announce a widely-expected privatisation programme.

"We had hoped that the 1997 national budget would advance the reforms, which were initiated two years ago, but that did not happen," said Christopher Kolade, chairman of food giant Cadbury Nigeria Plc at the company's annual general meeting last week.

"With little activity within the economy, the government holding back spending on infrastructure and other development and internal debts not being paid, there has been little to cheer about in the year to date," he added.

Instead, Africa's leading oil producer with a steady source of foreign income, set out a reflationary package for new capital projects and local debt repayment to engineer economic growth from within. But so far, no votes have been released.

According to national planning minister Ayo Ogunlade, the government deliberately held back releasing the capital grant for the first and second quarters because it needed to consolidate on the economic stability of 1996.
"It would have been disastrous if we had released the votes by February or shortly after the budget announcement," he said.
He said government would start to release capital grants as soon as it was convinced macro-economic stability would not be disrupted by pumping money into the system.

Signs of trouble with the reflationary package, aimed at achieving 5.5-percent economic growth compared with 3.3 percent, also emerged in March when Nigeria was forced to devalue the naira by 5.88 percent.

The government says there will be no more devaluations and so far, has been able to bring down demand at the weekly forex auction to about $45 million at last week's sale compared to $100 million weekly when it was forced to devalue.
